title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
abstract_summary: This paper introduces 'generative agents', computational software agents that simulate believable human behavior. The authors propose an architecture that extends large language models to store a complete record of an agent's experiences in natural language. This memory is synthesized over time into higher-level reflections and retrieved dynamically to inform behavior. The architecture is instantiated in a sandbox environment inspired by The Sims, populated by twenty-five agents. Evaluations demonstrate that these agents produce believable individual and emergent social behaviors, such as autonomously spreading invitations to a party. The work highlights the potential for these agents in interactive applications while discussing ethical risks.
problem_and_motivation: The core problem is the lack of computational agents capable of simulating long-term, coherent human behavior in open-world environments. While large language models (LLMs) can simulate human behavior at a single point in time, they struggle with long-term coherence because they lack mechanisms to manage growing memories, reflect on past experiences, and apply those insights to future actions. Existing approaches, such as rule-based systems or reinforcement learning, are either too rigid or limited to adversarial games with well-defined rewards. The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating agents that can remember, retrieve, reflect, and plan, thereby enabling more believable, persistent, and socially dynamic simulations.
contributions: Introduction of generative agents: believable simulacra of human behavior conditioned on dynamic experiences.
A novel agent architecture that enables agents to remember, retrieve, reflect, and plan through evolving circumstances.
Two evaluations (controlled and end-to-end) establishing the causal importance of the architecture's components.
Discussion of ethical and societal risks, including parasocial relationships, deepfakes, and over-reliance on AI in design processes.

method.overview: The architecture combines a large language model (ChatGPT) with three core components: a memory stream, reflection, and planning. The memory stream acts as a long-term database of all agent experiences. The reflection mechanism periodically synthesizes these experiences into higher-level inferences. The planning mechanism translates these inferences and the current environment into actionable, long-term plans. These components are recursively fed back into the memory stream to influence future behavior.

components.name: Memory Stream
components.description: A database that maintains a comprehensive record of an agent's experiences in natural language. It consists of 'observations' (events directly perceived). A retrieval function surfaces relevant memories based on a weighted combination of recency, importance, and relevance. Recency uses an exponential decay function; importance is generated by the LLM; relevance is calculated via cosine similarity of embedding vectors.
components.equations_or_algorithms: score = alpha_recency * recency + alpha_importance * importance + alpha_relevance * relevance

components.name: Reflection
components.description: A mechanism that synthesizes raw observations into higher-level, abstract thoughts. Periodically, when the sum of importance scores of recent events exceeds a threshold, the agent identifies salient questions about its experiences. It then queries the memory stream for relevant records and uses the LLM to generate insights, which are stored as new reflections in the memory stream.

components.name: Planning
components.description: A top-down process that translates an agent's goals and background into a sequence of actions. It starts with a broad daily plan, which is then recursively decomposed into hour-long chunks and further into 5-15 minute granular actions. Plans are stored in the memory stream and can be updated or re-planned if the agent perceives new, relevant information.

method.settings: Implementation uses gpt-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT). The sandbox environment is built using the Phaser web game framework. The simulation involved 25 agents over two game days.

tasks_and_datasets.name: Controlled Evaluation (Interview)
tasks_and_datasets.description: Agents were interviewed across five categories (self-knowledge, memory, plans, reactions, reflections) to assess their ability to maintain character and coherence.

tasks_and_datasets.name: End-to-End Evaluation
tasks_and_datasets.description: A two-day simulation of 25 agents in Smallville to observe emergent social behaviors (information diffusion, relationship formation, coordination).
tasks_and_datasets.metric: Percentage of agents with information, network density, successful coordination (party attendance)

baselines: No observation, no reflection, no planning (fully ablated)
No reflection, no planning (access to observations only)
No reflection (access to observations and plans)
experiments.setup_details: 100 human evaluators recruited from Prolific. Within-subjects design where evaluators ranked the believability of responses from different architectures. TrueSkill used to convert ranks to interval data.

results.comparison: Full architecture vs. ablated versions vs. human baseline
results.numbers: Full architecture: 29.89; No reflection: 26.88; No reflection/planning: 25.64; Human: 22.95; Fully ablated: 21.21
results.takeaway: The full architecture significantly outperforms all ablated conditions and the human baseline.

results.comparison: Start of simulation vs. end of simulation
results.numbers: Mayoral candidacy knowledge: 4% to 32%; Party invitation knowledge: 4% to 52%

claims_table.claim: Full architecture produces more believable behavior than ablated versions.

ablations_and_analysis.what_varied: Access to memory, reflection, and planning
ablations_and_analysis.finding: Each component contributes critically to believability; removing them degrades performance.
ablations_and_analysis.numbers: Full (29.89) > No Reflection (26.88) > No Reflection/Planning (25.64) > Fully Ablated (21.21)

limitations: Synthesizing large memory sets poses challenges for retrieval and action selection.
Agents may choose less typical locations as they learn about more places.
Misclassification of physical norms (e.g., bathroom occupancy, store hours).
Instruction tuning can lead to overly formal or overly cooperative behavior.
High computational cost (thousands of dollars in tokens for a 2-day simulation).
Potential for hallucination or memory embellishment.
Vulnerability to prompt hacking and memory hacking.
failure_modes: Inheriting overly formal speech from the LLM.
Erratic behavior due to misinterpreting physical environment norms.
future_work: Fine-tuning relevance, recency, and importance functions.
Parallelizing agents or developing specialized LLMs for generative agents.
Longer-term evaluation to establish rigorous benchmarks.
Aligning underlying LLM values to mitigate bias.

key_claims.claim: Generative agents can produce believable individual and emergent social behaviors.
The proposed architecture (memory, reflection, planning) is critical for long-term coherence.

definitions_and_terms.meaning: Computational software agents that simulate believable human behavior by leveraging large language models and a memory/reflection/planning architecture.
A long-term memory module that records a comprehensive list of an agent's experiences in natural language.
A mechanism that synthesizes raw observations into higher-level, abstract thoughts to guide future behavior.

related_work_positioning: The authors position their work within the long-standing goal of creating believable agents (e.g., Bates 1994, Laird and vanLent 2001). They contrast their approach with rule-based systems (e.g., finite-state machines, behavior trees) and reinforcement learning, arguing that these are either too rigid or limited to adversarial games. They build upon recent advancements in LLMs (e.g., Social Simulacra, Park et al. 2022) by adding a persistent, structured memory and reflection architecture to address the lack of long-term coherence in previous LLM-based agent attempts.

sections_summary.summary: Introduces the vision of creating believable computational agents that act consistently with past experiences. Defines generative agents and the core architecture components: memory, reflection, and planning.
Reviews literature on human-AI interaction, believable agents, and the use of LLMs for simulating human behavior. Identifies the gap in long-term coherence and memory management.
Describes the Smallville sandbox environment, how agents communicate, and provides examples of emergent social behaviors like information diffusion and coordination.
Details the technical architecture: the memory stream (retrieval via recency, importance, relevance), reflection (synthesizing memories), and planning (top-down decomposition).
Explains the technical implementation using the Phaser framework and how the environment is grounded in natural language for the agents.
Describes the interview-based evaluation comparing the full architecture against various ablations and a human baseline, showing the full architecture is most believable.
Details the two-day simulation in Smallville, measuring emergent social outcomes like information diffusion, relationship formation, and group coordination.
Discusses applications, future work, limitations (e.g., cost, hallucinations), and ethical/societal risks (e.g., parasocial relationships, over-reliance).
